420.bp: Imagine you're hiring someone but candidates arrive one at a time in random order, and you have to decide on the spot whether to hire each person before the next one shows up. The goal is to pick the single best or near-best person. This mirrors real problems like renting an apartment, buying a house, or selecting a supplier when options appear unpredictably.
420.wh: The problem is that you can't rewind: once you pass on someone, they're gone forever. The classical math for this situation (the '1/e law') guarantees you'll do within 37% of the best possible outcome if you could see everyone first, but that 37% gap feels large. We want a tighter promise about how badly you could do, not just a worst-case ratio.
420.ap: Instead of measuring success as a ratio against the best hindsight pick, they measure it as an absolute gap in value. They then show that a family of algorithms called 'pricing curves'—which set decision thresholds that change as more candidates arrive—can keep that absolute gap down to at most 0.25 out of a possible 1. A tighter variant, 'best-only pricing curves,' cuts it further to 0.19.
420.ww: The reason this works is that pricing curves adapt to what you've seen so far. As candidates arrive and reveal their values, the algorithms learn whether standards should stay high or drop—you're not locked into a rigid rule. This flexibility lets you avoid the regret of hiring too early or passing on someone good while waiting for someone perfect who never comes.
420.po: The paper proves these algorithms achieve a regret bound of 0.19 (or 0.25 for the broader class) and shows no policy can do better than 0.152 overall. This gives practitioners a concrete handle on how much value they'll sacrifice when making hiring or selection decisions in uncertain, streamed settings.

421.bp: Machine learning models in the real world face a sneaky threat: an attacker flips a training label here and there—labeling 'cat' as 'dog'—to poison the model's learned behavior. The damage feels severe but random, except it isn't. Some classes suffer far more than others, and understanding why matters for defense.
421.wh: Most research assumes attacks damage all classes equally. But the paper reveals the hidden truth: classes that are inherently hard to tell apart (like 'dog' and 'wolf' in images) get hurt much more by label flips than classes that are obviously different (like 'dog' and 'airplane'). Why? Because when classes blur together already, a wrong label just reinforces that blur rather than creating a contradiction.
421.ap: The authors prove mathematically that vulnerability lives in the feature-space separation between classes. Classes sitting close together in feature space are easy targets. They then propose CACL, a training method that explicitly pushes the most vulnerable class pairs farther apart in the feature space, making it harder for mislabels to fool the model.
421.ww: The intuition is simple: if your model learns to represent 'dog' and 'wolf' features very differently—maximizing the gap between them—then mislabeling a wolf as a dog stands out as a contradiction the model can't smoothly rationalize. You've made confusion costly and obvious.
421.po: Experiments confirm that class separability predicts vulnerability, and CACL protects the most at-risk class pairs while maintaining accuracy on others. This means defenses can be surgical: focus your effort on the truly vulnerable spots rather than building uniform armor.

422.bp: Training deep learning models burns enormous energy and carbon. Companies often compress datasets into tiny synthetic replacements to train faster and cheaper—a technique called dataset distillation. The catch: a synthetic dataset distilled for one type of model (say, a convolutional network) often fails when you try to use it to train a different type (say, a vision transformer). This forces wasteful re-distillation each time.
422.wh: Current distillation methods inadvertently bake in details about the specific architecture used during compression. The synthetic data gets optimized for that architecture's particular quirks—its biases—so when a different architecture tries to learn from the same synthetic data, it's like giving someone a manual written for a left-handed person but they're right-handed. The method solves the problem for CNN but breaks for ViT.
422.ap: The authors reframe model-agnosticism using information theory. They want to create synthetic data that removes the signature of any particular model. They cast this as a game: one player creates synthetic data, another player tries to guess which original architecture it came from. If the second player fails, the synthetic data is truly architecture-neutral. They turn this game into a concrete algorithm that minimizes mutual information between the synthetic data and the model type.
422.ww: This game-like adversarial approach forces the synthetic data to wash away architectural signatures. By making it impossible to predict which model was used, you're guaranteeing the data doesn't contain hidden clues that help only one architecture. It's like writing instructions so clear and unbiased that anyone—left-handed or right-handed—can follow them equally well.
422.po: Tests on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet show AMID works across CNNs and vision transformers with strong accuracy at just 1% of the original dataset size, matching or beating specialized methods. This cuts energy waste by eliminating redundant re-distillations and keeps the green AI promise alive.

423.bp: Search engines and recommendation systems decide what information reaches billions of people each day. Bias in these systems—showing different results to different groups unfairly—can harm communities and warp public discourse. Yet 'fairness' is slippery to define and measure. The goal is a coherent framework to think about fairness across all these systems.
423.wh: Fairness in information retrieval is messy because it involves many moving parts: the retriever, the items being ranked, the users, the providers supplying the items. Are you being unfair to the user (hiding what they need) or the provider (suppressing their content)? Is the harm instantaneous or does it compound over time? Classic fairness definitions from machine learning don't capture this web-scale complexity where thousands of actors interact.
423.ap: The authors draw an analogy to economics. An information retrieval system is really a market: users are buyers of information, content providers are sellers, and the ranking algorithm is the market mechanism. They organize fairness concepts into a three-dimensional cube: macro vs. micro (system-level harm vs. individual-level), demand vs. supply (user-facing vs. provider-facing), and short-term vs. long-term effects. Each fairness algorithm can be placed in this cube.
423.ww: Economics already has language and theory for these multi-stakeholder problems. By mapping IR fairness onto economics—distinguishing producer welfare from consumer welfare, immediate effects from equilibrium effects—you get a structured vocabulary. You realize that 'fair ranking' might sacrifice user experience for publisher diversity, or vice versa, and you can talk about the tradeoff honestly.
423.po: The framework provides a common language to discuss past fairness work and to spot gaps. Practitioners and researchers can now say 'this algorithm optimizes macro demand fairness' or 'that one balances supply short-term and long-term'—making explicit what was implicit, helping the field progress more systematically.

424.bp: On X (formerly Twitter), Community Notes lets volunteers from different political sides collectively mark which posts are misleading. It's an elegant crowdsourced fact-checking system. But once a note is labeled 'helpful' and shown to millions, the crowd's opinion can shift. Understanding these shifts matters because unstable labels erode trust in the system.
424.wh: The paper discovers a harsh dynamic: when a note becomes visible, people rally around it or against it in polarized ways. If you already agree with the note's framing, you rate it helpful more often. If you disagree, you rate it unhelpful. The note's initial 'helpful' status can trigger a cascade of new ratings from opponents that flip the verdict, causing the note to disappear. This post-display polarization is predictable but destabilizing.
424.ap: The authors analyzed 437,000 notes and 35 million ratings from over 580,000 contributors. They used interrupted time series analysis to measure what happens the moment a note goes public: rating volume spikes, and the direction of ratings shifts sharply based on whether a rater agrees with the note. They found that 30% of notes displayed as 'helpful' later lose that status, usually driven by opposing raters.
424.ww: The mechanism is psychological and structural: visibility brings attention, attention attracts both supporters and opponents, and online platforms amplify disagreement. Once a note is exposed, skeptics mobilize faster or in greater numbers than passive supporters, reversing what looked like stable consensus. The algorithm worked to select initially-helpful notes, but didn't account for how visibility itself changes the voting dynamic.
424.po: The findings expose a vulnerability in consensus-based systems: they assume voting is stable, but display itself destabilizes votes. Roughly a third of 'helpful' notes disappear after display, primarily due to polarized rating behavior. This suggests misinformation systems need post-display moderation, visibility gating, or rating credibility weighting to protect consensus from being sabotaged by organized opposition.

425.bp: Factories and power plants use thousands of sensors to track machinery health in real time. The dream is to predict failures before they happen and schedule repairs. But sensors create a data deluge—so much information flowing so fast that processing it all centrally (in a cloud data center) is expensive and too slow. You need instant decisions at the factory edge, but without the brainpower of cloud analysis.
425.wh: The core tension is that simple edge computers can flag anomalies quickly but unreliably. They might cry wolf on noisy data and create false alarms that cost money. Cloud systems are smarter but far away—data must travel, creating latency that defeats the point of early warning. Also, humans and other systems downstream need to understand why the anomaly was flagged, not just get a binary alert.
425.ap: ECLAD splits the job smartly: lightweight edge code screens for obvious anomalies in the stream of sensor readings. When something seems off, it sends that data to the cloud for a smarter model (a sequence model trained on longer histories) to verify. If verified as truly anomalous, a large language model kicks in to write a natural language explanation—'the compressor vibration spiked at 3 PM after temperature rose 10 degrees'—and learns from past cases to refine its classification scheme.
425.ww: This three-stage pipeline works because each stage handles what it's best at: edge handles speed and real-time screening, cloud handles accuracy through deeper models, and the language model handles human understanding through explanation. You avoid forcing edge computers to be both fast and precise, and you avoid sending all data to the cloud. The explanations also let humans spot if the system is drifting.
425.po: The end-to-end system shows real-time responsiveness with high-precision anomaly detection and human-readable reports through a web interface. The 'self-evolving anomaly tree' means the system learns from corrections, reducing retraining burden. Predictive maintenance teams can now trust an alert, understand it, and act fast.

426.bp: Many real-world datasets are structured as graphs—social networks, citation webs, knowledge bases—where each node (a person, a paper, a concept) has text attached. Training a full neural network and language model jointly on million-node graphs is slow and wasteful. The goal is to compress the graph down to tiny synthetic version that trains equally well, saving energy and time.
426.wh: Most graph compression methods ignore the text. They compress only the structure (the connections). But text-attributed graphs are twice as hard: you must compress both the text descriptions and the topology while preserving what the joint model learns. Text compression is novel to this problem. Also, existing compression methods that match training trajectories (the path of improving accuracy during training) suffer from high variance—different random seeds produce wildly different compressed graphs.
426.ap: TAGSAM uses two parallel strategies. For text: it selects representative chunks from descriptions of related nodes and merges them, picking chunks that carry maximum information (information maximization). For graph structure: instead of directly matching training trajectories, it aligns similarity matrices—stable representations of which nodes are 'close'—avoiding the high variance of trajectory matching.
426.ww: The two-part design respects the dual nature of the problem. Text selection via mutual information maximization keeps only the unique signal from descriptions. The similarity-matrix matching is more stable because it focuses on static structural relationships rather than the noisy trajectory of training. Together, they preserve what the model actually uses: semantic content and relational structure.
426.po: On CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, TAGSAM compresses graphs to 1% of original size with only 4.9% accuracy loss compared to the best competitor. The method generalizes across different neural architectures and languages, making the compressed dataset truly reusable instead of model-specific.

427.bp: News travels fast online, but spotting trends early is harder than you'd think. Trending detection usually waits for people to search—'what's everyone looking for?'—but by the time search volume rises, millions have already missed the story. In low-traffic contexts (rare or long-tail topics), there's no search signal at all. The goal is to predict what will trend before anyone searches.
427.wh: The cold-start problem is real: without search queries, you have no signal. News posts and posts arrive constantly, but they sit invisible until search volume emerges, and by then it's stale. Keyword frequency in posts is slow and fragile. You need a way to simulate search queries from posts themselves, then score which synthetic queries will matter. But language models drift over time—what seemed important last week might not be important this week.
427.ap: RTTP generates search queries directly from news content using a continual-learning language model. It scores each synthetic query by combining engagement strength (how many likes/shares/comments) with creator authority (how influential is the person posting). As new content arrives and trends shift, the model retrains continuously. But continuous retraining risks 'catastrophic forgetting'—the model forgets how to generate good queries from earlier patterns. So the authors propose Mix-Policy DPO, a preference learning technique that blends on-policy training (keeping what worked) with off-policy exploration (discovering new patterns).
427.ww: By generating synthetic search queries, you're creating signal where none existed. The engagement + authority scoring prioritizes content that matters socially, not just what's being discussed. Continual learning lets the model adapt weekly. Mix-Policy DPO keeps the model stable (remembering what worked) while allowing evolution (learning new trends), avoiding the oscillation or collapse that usually happens with naive retraining.
427.po: Deployed at Facebook and Meta, RTTP achieves 91.4% improvement in tail-trend detection precision and 19% better query generation accuracy than baselines. The system sustains stable performance through multi-week online retraining, turning latent signals in content into early-warning trend predictions.

428.bp: Video captioning—automatically writing a sentence or two describing a video—sounds simple but is hard because you must understand both visual motion and semantic meaning, then align them into coherent language. A caption must match the video's action and significance. Getting this right matters for search, accessibility, and video understanding systems.
428.wh: Most methods focus on extracting visual features (objects, motion) but treat language as an afterthought. They ignore the rich semantic links between what you see and what words mean. A video of 'a person running in a park' could be tagged 'exercise', 'outdoor activity', or 'jogging', but which fits best requires understanding how visual concepts and language concepts relate. Naive methods miss these cross-modal relationships.
428.ap: MGCDVc uses two ideas together: a graph-based semantic model and a diffusion-based generation model. It creates latent 'concept anchors'—abstract bridges between visual features and language—then builds a weighted graph connecting visual nodes, textual nodes, and anchors. It then generates the caption by working through this graph structure, where each word-node and its connections are revealed gradually, like diffusion filling in a picture pixel by pixel. A soft pruning mechanism removes low-quality nodes, cleaning up the graph.
428.ww: Graphs capture relationships: which visual elements relate to which concepts, which words co-occur naturally. Diffusion-based generation respects these relationships gradually instead of predicting all words at once. This structured generation is more coherent because each new word is aware of the graph context, not just previous words. Pruning keeps the reasoning lean by discarding noisy, unhelpful nodes.
428.po: On standard benchmarks, MGCDVc improves caption accuracy and relevance by incorporating relational reasoning. The graph-conditioned diffusion approach produces more semantically coherent captions than methods that treat visual and language features independently, especially on complex scenes with multiple actions.

429.bp: Cryptocurrencies like Ethereum host decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms where users lend and borrow money recorded as immutable on-chain transactions. These platforms are a rich source of temporal data: when do users deposit? When do they withdraw? When do defaults (non-payment) happen? Understanding these patterns—predicting who will churn or default—is crucial for platform stability. The field needs rigorous benchmarks to measure progress.
429.wh: Temporal prediction on Web3 is different from typical prediction: the data is public but sparse, transactions are recorded with exact timestamps but users' true intent is hidden, and the system evolves rapidly as new features arrive. Traditional benchmarks from web analytics don't capture this mix of sparsity, real-world censoring (some users disappear; you don't know if they quit or just went dormant), and non-stationarity (the system's behavior changes over time as adoption grows).
429.ap: The FinSurvival Challenge 2025 analyzed 21.8 million transactions from Aave v3, a major lending protocol. It defined 16 survival-prediction tasks: given a user's early activity, predict whether they'll still be active later (or default, or reduce activity). Winning solutions built domain-aware features—things like 'collateral volatility' and 'historical interest-rate sensitivity'—that generic time-series methods miss. The challenge published the dataset and evaluated reproducible results.
429.ww: Domain-aware features work because they encode the specific risks and incentives in DeFi: users care about collateral safety, interest rates matter differently than in traditional finance, and transaction costs drive behavior. A system agnostic to these realities—just looking at 'time since deposit'—misses key signals. The benchmark enforced reproducibility, spotting which methods generalize and which overfit.
429.po: The benchmark surfaces that temporal feature engineering (understanding DeFi mechanics) beats generic time-series models. This provides a foundation for measuring progress on Web3 prediction and a sandbox for testing techniques relevant to broader temporal analytics—churn, risk, evolution—that appear everywhere online.

430.bp: Planning a trip is tedious: you search blogs, articles, and reviews, then manually stitch together an itinerary day by day. The dream is an interactive tool that generates itineraries on the fly by reading current travel content and adapting to your preferences. A smart, controllable travel assistant would save hours.
430.wh: Travel blogs and articles are scattered, unstructured, and constantly changing. Each one covers different attractions with different depths. Extracting a coherent itinerary requires: fetching fresh content, distilling key attractions, reasoning about logistics (travel time between sites, opening hours), and ranking by user interest. No single off-the-shelf tool handles all steps, and cloud APIs are slow for interactive use.
430.ap: Roamify is a browser extension that runs end-to-end on your computer without hitting external servers. It scrapes current travel blogs, summarizes them using a finetuned T5 model to extract key attractions and descriptions, then generates a multi-day itinerary using LLaMA 3 language model. The user controls sliders encoding preferences: historical sites, natural parks, cultural landmarks, amusement parks. The LLM uses these sliders to rank and sequence attractions into a coherent plan.
430.ww: Client-side processing is crucial: no round-trip to a server, so responses feel instant. Finetuned summarization keeps extraction fast and domain-focused. Preference sliders make the system controllable—instead of a generic itinerary, you get one tuned to your interests. The language model acts as a reasoning engine, avoiding rigid rules ('do cultural sites before museums') and adapting to the actual content available.
430.po: Roamify demonstrates a complete pipeline: live data retrieval, neural summarization, preference modeling, and on-device language model inference. Users get interactive, up-to-date itineraries in seconds, with transparency (no cloud uploads) and control (sliders adjust recommendations), showcasing how language models can power real-time web intelligence applications.

431.bp: Detecting large-scale cyberattacks—a 'super host' sending traffic to thousands of distinct targets, or a victim host flooded by thousands of sources—is vital for network defense. ISPs and defenders use high-speed sketches (compact data structures that track patterns in data streams) to spot these threats without storing all traffic. The challenge is doing this accurately on real-world data with limited memory.
431.wh: Existing sketch-based approaches count distinct IP addresses as the sole signal of a super host. But attackers and botnets are smarter: they often communicate within the same subnet (the same geographic block of IP addresses, like 192.168.1.x). A naive 'distinct IP count' gives false positives—multiple hosts on one subnet look like one super host—and misses concentrated attacks within a subnet. Fixing this with hierarchical structures wastes memory.
431.ap: SegSketch introduces a 'halved-segment hashing' strategy that estimates the common prefix length of IP addresses without storing full addresses. Common prefixes reveal subnet relationships cheaply. The algorithm estimates cardinality (distinct count) within subnets, not across all addresses. This hybrid approach keeps memory low while capturing subnet-aware signals that naive full-address counting misses.
431.ww: The core insight is that attackers cluster geographically in IP space. By detecting that cluster structure—noticing that thousands of targets share a common subnet prefix—you identify real attacks, not noise. Halved-segment hashing efficiently infers prefix lengths without storing full IPs, so you get subnet awareness at sketch-level memory cost.
431.po: Real-world traces show SegSketch improves F1-score (a balance between false positives and false negatives) by up to 8x over state-of-the-art solutions, especially on tight memory budgets. This means network defenders can spot super hosts more reliably, reducing false alarms while catching real attacks.

432.bp: Social networks and online communities are structured as graphs of people and connections, often with text (posts, profiles). Detecting misinformation, toxic behavior, or other harms requires analyzing this graph. Large language models show promise for reasoning over such graphs, but you need labeled examples to teach them. Obtaining expert labels for sensitive content—'is this post misinformation?'—is slow, costly, and often impossible at scale.
432.wh: Instruction tuning, the standard way to adapt language models to graph tasks, requires many (INSTRUCTION, OUTPUT) pairs from labeled nodes. In social networks, labels are scarce: experts can label a few hundred posts, but the graph has millions. Standard methods ignore unlabeled nodes despite their relational structure. Labeled and unlabeled nodes are connected, and those connections carry signal, but naive supervised learning throws that signal away.
432.ap: SIT-Graph uses self-training: the model is initially finetuned on scarce labeled data, then iteratively improved by having it label unlabeled nodes and retraining on its own predictions (carefully, to avoid error accumulation). The key novelty is that instruction tuning (crafting task-specific prompts) is maintained throughout, not just at initialization. The method is model-agnostic; it works with any graph instruction-tuning approach.
432.ww: Self-training exploits the structure: if two unlabeled nodes are connected and one is mislabeled, nearby nodes' correct labels will eventually pull the model back. By carefully iterating—the model labels high-confidence examples, gets retrained, and refines its understanding—you bootstrap from few labels to strong performance. Maintaining instruction tuning throughout keeps the model reasoning in natural language, more interpretable than black-box features.
432.po: SIT-Graph reduces the need for labeled data while leveraging the full graph structure, making it practical to deploy LLMs on social networks for moderation and misinformation detection despite annotation scarcity. The self-training approach sustains performance across iterations, enabling sensitive applications where expert labels are limited.

433.bp: NFTs (non-fungible tokens) are digital assets—art, collectibles, virtual real estate—stored on blockchains. Their value proposition is permanence and decentralization: because they're on an immutable blockchain, you own them forever and can't be censored. But this promise depends on where the actual content lives. If the image or metadata is stored on a centralized server, that server can disappear, taking your asset with it.
433.wh: The inconvenient truth: most NFTs store actual content (images, videos) off-chain on servers like Amazon S3 or IPFS gateways operated by a single entity. The blockchain stores only a link—a pointer—to that content. If the server goes down, the link is worthless and your 'permanent' digital art is gone. High-value NFTs are often stored this way because blockchain storage is expensive, creating a 'Blue-chip Trap': the most valuable assets are the most fragile.
433.ap: The authors collected 16 million real NFTs and systematically audited their storage. They traced where each asset's content actually sits: centralized servers, fragile IPFS nodes, or truly decentralized systems. They found eight distinct vulnerabilities: access failures (server down), tamperability (server owner modifies content), and forgeability (attacker replaces content with a fake). They mapped real assets to this taxonomy and scored severity using CVSS (the industry standard for security vulnerability severity).
433.ww: The mismatch between promise and reality exposes a fundamental tension: immutability and decentralization are expensive at scale, so the industry took shortcuts. A blockchain transaction costs pennies but storing a megabyte of image data costs dollars, so builders stored only pointers. This works until the pointer breaks. The analysis shows these aren't theoretical risks—they're widespread, measurable defects affecting millions of high-value assets.
433.po: The taxonomy reveals eight classes of storage defects with severity scores. All pose substantial risks. The findings give developers concrete guidance on secure storage: use truly decentralized systems or redundancy, not single centralized servers. For users, it's a cautionary tale: 'permanent' NFTs aren't always permanent, and the most valuable ones are often the most at-risk.

434.bp: Ads and tracking scripts follow you across the web, profiling your behavior and serving targeted ads. Blocking them protects privacy and cuts bloat. Adblocker extensions detect and filter these scripts. But as ad networks evolve to evade blockers—obfuscating code, changing domain names, using new delivery methods—static filter lists fall behind. A smarter, learned system that adapts to evasion would be more resilient.
434.wh: Current machine learning ad blockers use features easily evaded by attackers: if the model learns 'URLs with pattern X are ads', attackers simply avoid pattern X. Adversarial attacks can fool detectors with small perturbations: changing a few characters in code or slightly modifying a domain name breaks detection (57-92% evasion rates reported). Also, models trained on one site's ads generalize poorly to others, and accuracy degrades over time as new ad techniques emerge, requiring expensive retraining.
434.ap: AdVersa uses hard-to-perturb features: embeddings from code (the actual script content) and URLs that capture deep semantic meaning, not surface patterns. The model is trained on a large 2.74M-request dataset and deployed on the client side (in your browser), never calling home. A pseudo-labeling strategy lets the model improve continuously on new traffic without manual retraining: it labels high-confidence new examples, learns from them, and adapts.
434.ww: Code and URL embeddings extract semantic patterns that survive minor perturbations. An attacker must rewrite logic or change domains substantially to evade, not just tweak surface text. Client-side deployment means the model sees and adapts to real traffic in real time. Pseudo-labeling reduces drift without annotation overhead—the model bootstraps corrections from its own confident predictions.
434.po: AdVersa achieves 98.23% F1 score, twice the robustness against adversarial attacks compared to baselines, and strong cross-domain generalization (91.47% F1 on unseen sites). Maintenance overhead drops by 99.8% through pseudo-labeling, eliminating the burden of curating filter lists or retraining. The lightweight client-side design protects privacy while delivering state-of-the-art blocking.
